messages.subject: bug in NIMBLE bootstrap particle filter
messages.subject_clean: bug in NIMBLE bootstrap particle filter
messages.body_plain:
All,

We recently discovered a bug in the numerical implementation of
NIMBLE's bootstrap particle filter. The bug omitted inclusion of the
weights from the previous iteration when calculating the new weights
after an iteration in which resampling was not done. Thus it has
affected any use of the bootstrap filter where the 'thresh' argument
is less than one (including use of the default 'thresh' value of 0.8).

Given that the bootstrap filter is the default filter in NIMBLE's
particle MCMC, the bug would have affected default use of NIMBLE's
particle MCMC sampler. The particle MCMC sampler is never
automatically assigned in an MCMC but is used
when a user assigns  the 'RW_PF' or 'RW_PF_block' sampler.

We've fixed the bug in the recently released version 0.6-12 of NIMBLE.
We apologize for the error and strongly encourage anyone who has used
the bootstrap filter to redo their calculations using the updated
version of NIMBLE.

Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

messages.subject_clean: WAIC calculations for multistate capture-recapture models
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

mostly out of curiosity, I have tried to calculate WAIC for a multistate mark-recapture model I have been working with. WAIC always calculations returned "NaN", irrespective of whether I used the wrapper function nimbleMCMC(..., WAIC = TRUE) or buildt the model stepwise (via nimbleModel(...) --> configureMCMC(...) --> buildMCMC(..., enableWAIC = TRUE) --> compileNimble(...) --> model$run() --> model$WAIC()).

Running the model uncompiled did not produce any helpful warning/error messages, so I tried it on some simple examples from BPA ("Bayesian Population Analysis using WinBUGS", Kery & Schaub 2011) and/or modified versions of them from the Nimble workshop in April 2018.
(All codes and example data - if required - are attached here).

In short, I found this:

1) Dipper example (BPA Ch.7), CJS formulation: WAIC calculations return a number.
2) Dipper example, reformulated as 2-state multistate CR model: WAIC calculations return a number.
3) Plover example (BPA Ch.9), 3-state multistate CR model: WAIC calculations return "NaN"
4) Orchid example (BPA Ch.9), 4-state multistate CR model: WAIC calculations return "NaN"

Based on this, it looks like WAIC calculations fail for multistate CR models with more than 2 states. Why would that happen? Is there a way to find out exactly at which step of WAIC calculations things go wrong?

Any help much appreciated.
Cheers,

Chloé

messages.subject: WAIC differences
messages.body_plain:
I have been developing space-time models using NIMBLE based on conversions from OpenBUGS. Spatial models work well and the ST models also run fine.
 However I have found that there are quite large differences in WAIC values reported when using
nimbleMCMC compared to the runMCMC.

In the example I developed the main code is:

LST<-nimbleModel(code=STCode,name="LST",constants=LSTConsts,
data=LSTdata,inits=LSTinits)
LSTConf<-configureMCMC(LST,print=TRUE)
LSTConf$addMonitors(c("a0","g","u","v","theta"))
LSTMCMC<-buildMCMC(LSTConf)
CLSTMCMC<-compileNimble(LSTMCMC,project=LST)
niter<-20000
set.seed(1)
samples<-runMCMC(CLSTMCMC,niter=niter,nburnin=15000,nchains=1,summary=TRUE,WAIC=TRUE,samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE)
samples$summary
samples$WAIC

###### can also do a single call  ###########################
mcmc.out<-nimbleMCMC(code=STCode,constants=LSTConsts,
data=LSTdata,inits=LSTinits,nchains=1,nburnin=15000,niter=20000,summary=TRUE,WAIC=TRUE)
mcmc.out$summary
mcmc.out$WAIC

These calls use exactly the same data, inits, burnin, iterations and a single chain but yield large differences in WAIC:

nimbleMCMC gives 277923
whereas runMCMC gives 6017.36

Can anyone shed light ?

messages.subject: Re: WAIC differences
messages.body_plain:
Andrew, sorry for the delay in getting back to you.

I can't recreate the problem without a reproducible example, but do have an idea about what's happening. The very short answer is that (I suspect) when you specify the monitors:

LSTConf$addMonitors(c("a0","g","u","v","theta"))

in your first example above, it changes the WAIC value.

The longer explanation would be, the calculation of WAIC uses the posterior samples generated by the MCMC.  By default, NIMBLE's MCMC assigns monitors (and thus collects posterior samples) for all top-level parameters in the model.  So by default, the samples for those top-level parameters are used to calculate WAIC, and all other non-data stochastic nodes, typically latent state in a model, have their values "simulated" during these calculations.  That's what happens in your second example above, using nimbleMCMC().

In contrast, in your first example you add monitors also to several other (presumably not-top-level) nodes.  This causes posterior samples to be collected for those nodes, and therefore also used in the calculation of WAIC.  In some cases, using these values (as opposed to "simulated" values) can causes large differences in the resulting WAIC.

Anyway, I'd try removing that one line of code: LSTConf$addMonitors(...), and see if the WAIC values agree (to within statistical tolerance).

Thanks for posting the question.  Keep in touch.

Daniel

Hi Daniel/Chris

Thanks for the explanation. However this seems a little strange.

The WAIC, as far as I am aware, is meant to be a overall goodness of fit measure: an improved DIC if you like.

However the calculation of DIC or WAIC doesnt usually depend on nodes being monitored.

I assume by "monitored" it is meant that these nodes are available for further examination (posterior samples being kept)

I decided to compare models on INLA and using runMCMC on Nimble (as INLA computes the WAIC automatically).

I got very close results between the two packages for ST models (such as was run in the example code I sent).

Of course there could be some differences given the approximation method differences.

However, INLA produces a WAIC  of 5768.8 whereas runMCMC with monitors 5766.14.

I then tested the idea that the monitors affect the result: I removed a monitor item from the monitor list (an assigned variable and so not a stochastic node)

and the resulting WAIC was 6165.11.  This is clearly different.

There appears to be an issue of some sort with this WAIC calculation: I assume others will

wonder why the WAIC should vary with monitors when it is supposed to be a global GOF measure.

At the very least there should be some clarity in the documentation about how to obtain the correct global WAIC

Hi Andrew,

You're correct that by a node being "monitored", we mean that posterior samples of that node are being saved.  These posterior samples are then used to calculate the WAIC.

Following the discussion in Section 2.5 of  "Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models" by Gelman, Huang, and Vehtari (2014), the posterior predictive distribution that is used to calculate the WAIC is in fact not unique.  Different choices for the predictive distribution will in turn lead to different WAIC values being calculated.

In NIMBLE, we've attempted to give users control over the form of the predictive distribution for a model by calculating WAIC using the posterior samples from the monitored stochastic nodes, while simulating values for un-monitored stochastic nodes, conditioned on the posterior values of monitored stochastic nodes.  This allows a single model to potentially produce a range of WAIC values, depending on which nodes are monitored.

That having been said, we definitely acknowledge the potential for confusion that can arise here.  Most commonly, the WAIC is calculated using posterior samples of every stochastic node in the model - this is the global WAIC you mentioned above.  In NIMBLE, this global WAIC can be calculated by providing "monitors = model$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE, includeData = FALSE)" in a call to configureMCMC() or nimbleMCMC().    NIMBLE defaults to monitoring only all top-level stochastic nodes, so using e.g. nimbleMCMC() with the default monitors will potentially result in quite a different WAIC value than the global value, as you described above.

In light of this, we plan (in a future version of NIMBLE) to give a warning message whenever a user calculates a WAIC without having all of the stochastic nodes in their model monitored, as this can lead to potentially unintended calculations.

Thanks for providing your example and discussion!

Nick

messages.subject: 1-row matrices as stochastic nodes
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

This question is probably related to a previous question <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/nimble-users/knGeV6ghm6A> that I raised a while back but this time is concerns a particular case of ours where we have matrices as stochastic nodes.

We have written a custom distribution that defines the distribution for a stochastic matrix.  However this question is less to do with the custom distribution but more to do with the default behaviour of NIMBLE in automatically reducing the dimensionality of nodes when it identifies that an indexing series equates to '1:1'.  In our case, we have a series of matrices that are stored in a three-dimensional structure, lets call this 'myData[1:numMaxRows, 1:numCols, 1:numMatrices]'.  Each matrix has a differing number of rows so we pad each matrix with dummy rows so that we ensure a non-ragged array.  The correct upper row index is stored in an accompanying vector, let call this 'upperRowIndex[1:numMatrices]'.  Typically we then use these two structures together in the model code like such:

nimbleCode({
    # .... some previous code
    # Iterate over the matrices
    for(matrixIter in 1:numMatrices) {
        # Subset the matrices according to the relevant number of rows and relate the matrix
        # the custom distribution
        myData[1:upperRowIndex[1:numMatrices], 1:numCols, matrixIter] ~ myCustomDistribution(...)
    }
    # .... some later code
})

Doing things this way works fine if every element of 'upperRowIndex' is two or greater.  The moment one of the upper indeces are one then NIMBLE evaluates the '1:1' token as a scalar and considers the matrix as a vector instead (as it now indexed by two scalars and a vector).

Now we've adopted two different solutions to this problem:

1.  We add an extra parameter to 'myCustomDistribution' that tells it how many rows to read when calculating the likelihood and then not subsetting the rows on the left-hand side of the node declaration.
2.  We pad every matrix with an extra row and add one to every entry in the 'upperRowIndex' vector.  That way every matrix has at least two rows after subsetting.  We then just add code to 'myCustomDistribution' to ignore the last row when performing likelihood calculations.

Both of these potential solutions work OK but makes the model specification a little clunky.  I just wanted to post here to make sure that I wasn't missing something more obvious like a 'alwaysAVector' function that ensures that a '1:x' token is always considered a vector even if x = 1.  Something that could be used on the left-hand side of a node declaration like such:

nimbleCode({
    # .... some previous code
    # Iterate over the matrices
    for(matrixIter in 1:numMatrices) {
        # Subset the matrices according to the relevant number of rows and relate the matrix
        # the custom distribution
        myData[alwaysAVector(1:upperRowIndex[1:numMatrices]), 1:numCols, matrixIter] ~ myCustomDistribution(...)
    }
    # .... some later code
})

I was wondering whether it is desirable that instances of '1:1' token in indexing are interpreted as a scalar in NIMBLE code and result in scalar indexing (and thus reduction in dimensionality of the indexed object).  It seems like that would be unexpected behaviour in most cases as this would almost always come about in the indexing of ragged arrays anyway.  I appreciate that this mirrors R's behaviour (which is not always desirable there either) but in R this causes fewer problems because the objects are weakly typed and it is possible to sanity check the dimensionality of input object at run time in any custom functions that you write.

Thank you for all your help on this so far!  I'm definitely enjoying the extensibility of NIMBLE and you guys have put together a really impressive piece of software!

All the best,

Joe

messages.body_plain:
Got it.

NIMBLE provides a few ways for casting vectors as 1xN or Nx1 arrays, those being asCol(x) and asRow(x), but I'm 99% sure those only work in the NIMBLE DSL (that is, in the run function of nimbleFunctions), and would not work in model code.  So, I don't think there's any way to do it, the way you're thinking.

I have dealt with this sort of thing before, with custom distributions where an argument is a vector, but sometimes that vector has length = 1.  The easiest way I've found, which I have to say I think is pretty clean and painless, is essentially your suggestion #1.  That is,

(1) Don't worry about subsetting the rows at all.  Just always pass in:
myData[1:numMaxRows, 1:numCols, matrixIter] ~ myCustomDistribution(...)

(2) Add an additional scalar parameter to the custom distribution, just telling it how many rows this particular vector actually has:
myData[1:numMaxRows, 1:numCols, matrixIter] ~ myCustomDistribution(..., length = upperRowIndex[matrixIter])

Then, of course, pass "upperRowIndex" in as constants to your model, and define your custom distribution to take this additional scalar "length" parameter, and in the calculations, make use of x[1:length].

That's what I've done in the past, and it hasn't seemed to be too much trouble.

Yes, you've definitely hit one NIMBLE issue right on the head: the non-identifiability issues between scalars and length=1 vectors.

Let me know if this isn't clear in any way, or if you come across anything better.  Hope it helps.

Cheers,
Daniel

        L <- dim(a)[1]
        print('length = ', L)
        b <- a[L:1]
        print('reversed vector: ', b)
    }
)

Cnf <- compileNimble(Rnf)

f <- 1:5

Rnf(f)

Cnf(f)

        b <- a[index]
